private assignComponent(): void {
    const formula = this.getType()._formula as this;
    const isFormula = this === formula;
    if (!isFormula && this._component) return

    const Component = (props: Properties) => {
        let chemical = chemicalRegistry.get(Component) as this;
        let newChemical = false;
        if (!chemical || isFormula) {
            chemical = this.construct();
            chemical._component = Component;
            chemicalRegistry.set(Component as any, chemical);
            newChemical = true;
        }

        // Set up this component's update function
        const [, update] = useState({});
        
        // Update the subscription on EVERY render, not just in useEffect
        const updateChemical = () => {
            console.log('Update triggered from event');
            update({});
        };
        
        // Clear old subscription and add new one with fresh update function
        chemical.onUpdate.unsubscribe(updateChemical);
        chemical.onUpdate.subscribe(updateChemical);
        
        useEffect(() => {
            chemical.reactivate();
            
            return () => {
                chemical._onReceivingProps.clear();
                chemical._onRenderingView.clear();
                chemical._onRenderedView.clear();
                chemical.onUpdate.clear();
                if (chemical._component)
                    chemicalRegistry.delete(Component as any);
            };
        }, []);

        // Give subscribers the ability to weigh in on props
        let newProps = chemical.onReceivingProps.fire(props);
        props = newProps || props;

        // Bind the props to the associated fields that are prefixed with $
        chemical.bindProps(props);

        // Reactivate the initial properties to prepare for binding children
        chemical.reactivate();

        // Render the iniital view
        let view = chemical.view();

        // Give subscribers the ability to weigh after the view has been rendered
        const result = chemical.onRenderingView.fire({ props, view });
        view = result?.view || view;

        // Give subscribers the ability to weigh in after the event loop ends and the UI updates
        chemical.onRenderedView.fire({ props, view });

        return view
    }

    if (isFormula)
        formula._component = Component;
    if (!this._component)
        this._component = Component;
}

Move updateChemical outside of useEffect so it gets recreated with the fresh update function on every render
Unsubscribe the old handler and subscribe the new one on every render (outside useEffect)
Keep reactivate() in useEffect since that only needs to run once
This ensures that when the property changes and fires the update event, it's calling the current render'supdate function, not a stale one from the first render.

When the component unmounts (component is removed from the DOM)

  someEvent.subscribe(() => update({})); // <-- React says NO!

}

// GOOD - In effect:
function Component() {
  const [, update] = useState();
  useEffect(() => {
    someEvent.subscribe(() => update({})); // <-- React says OK!

  return <div>...</div>;

No, that won't work! hasMounted is a local variable that gets reset to false on every render. Each time Component runs, it creates a new hasMounted = false, so the subscription code will never execute.

The correct approach is to use useEffect:
typescript
private assignComponent(): void {
    const formula = this.getType().formula as this;
    const isFormula = this === formula;
    if (!isFormula && this._component) return

    const Component = (props: Properties) => {
        let chemical = chemicalRegistry.get(Component) as this;
        let newChemical = false;
        if (!chemical || isFormula) {
            chemical = this.construct();
            chemical._component = Component;
            chemicalRegistry.set(Component as any, chemical);
            newChemical = true;
        }

        // Set up this component's update function - ALWAYS call useState
        const [, update] = useState({});
        
        // Set up subscription in effect
        useEffect(() => {
            // Cleanup old subscription if exists
            if (chemical._updateToken)
                chemical.onUpdate.unsubscribe(chemical._updateToken);
            
            // Create new subscription
            chemical._updateToken = chemical.onUpdate.subscribe(() => update({}));
            
            // Reactivate the chemical
            chemical.reactivate();
            
            return () => {
                // Cleanup on unmount
                if (chemical._updateToken) {
                    chemical.onUpdate.unsubscribe(chemical._updateToken);
                    chemical._updateToken = undefined;
                }
            };
        }, []); // Run once per mount
        
        // Rest of the component logic...
    }
}
This ensures:
useState is always called (React requirement)
Subscription happens after mount (in useEffect)
Cleanup happens on unmount

    this.bonds = new Map();

    let chemical = this.chemical;
    const prototypes: any[] = [];
    while (chemical) {
        prototypes.unshift(chemical);
        if (chemical === $Chemical.prototype) break;
        chemical = Object.getPrototypeOf(chemical);
    }

    for (const prototype of prototypes) {
        // Use Object.getOwnPropertyNames to get ALL properties including getters/setters
        const propertyNames = Object.getOwnPropertyNames(prototype);
        for (const property of propertyNames) {
            const descriptor = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(prototype, property);
            const value = descriptor?.get ? undefined : prototype[property];
            if (!isReactiveProperty(prototype, property, value)) continue;
            this.configureBond(property, value, !this.initialized ? prototype[decoratorsKey] : undefined);
        }
    }
}
This way, computedProp will be discovered even though it's defined as a getter/setter, and a bond will be created for it.

private assignComponent(): void {
    const formula = this.getType().formula as this;
    const isFormula = this === formula;
    if (!isFormula && this._component) return

    const Component = (props: Properties) => {
        // Get or create instance counter for this component
        const instanceMap = useContext(ChemicalInstanceContext);
        let instanceNumber = instanceMap.get(Component) || 0;
        instanceMap.set(Component, instanceNumber + 1);

        const instanceKey = `${Component.name}-${instanceNumber}`;

            chemical = this.construct();
            chemical._component = Component;
            chemical._instanceId = instanceKey;
            chemical.reactivate();
            chemicalRegistry.set(instanceKey as any, chemical);
        }
        
        // Reset counter after render
        useEffect(() => {
            return () => {
                instanceMap.set(Component, 0);
            };
        }, []);
        
        // ... rest of component logic
    }

        if (chemical._updateToken)

        // Set up this component's update function
        const [, update] = useState({});

            return () => {
                chemical._onReceivingProps.clear();
                chemical._onRenderingView.clear();
                chemical._onRenderedView.clear();
                chemical.onUpdate.clear();
                if (chemical._component)
                    chemicalRegistry.delete(chemicalId as any);
            };
        }, []);

        // ... rest of component logic
    }
}

Here's a structured learning path for React fundamentals:
React Learning Topics
Core Hooks (Essential)
useState - Adds state to functional components; returns [value, setter] pair
useEffect - Runs side effects after render; handles lifecycle events like mount/unmount
useMemo - Memoizes expensive computations; recalculates only when dependencies change
useCallback - Memoizes functions to prevent recreation on every render
useRef - Creates mutable reference that persists across renders without triggering re-renders
useContext - Accesses React context values without prop drilling
Data Structures
Props object - Immutable object passed from parent; frozen at top level only
Children prop - Special prop containing nested JSX; can be elements, strings, arrays, or undefined
React elements - Plain objects describing what to render; created by JSX or React.createElement
React nodes - Valid render values: elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null, undefined
Component Lifecycle
Mount phase - Component first appears; state initialized, first render, effects run
Update phase - Props/state change triggers re-render; cleanup then re-run effects
Unmount phase - Component removed; cleanup functions run, refs cleared
State & Rendering
State binding - State is bound to component instance, not globally
Re-render triggers - State changes, prop changes, parent re-renders, context changes
Render phase vs commit phase - Calculate what changed vs actually update DOM
Advanced Patterns
Rules of Hooks - Only call at top level, only in React functions
Dependency arrays - Control when effects/memos recalculate
Cleanup functions - Return from useEffect to clean up subscriptions/timers
Which topic would you like to explore first? I recommend starting with useState since your framework relies heavily on state management.

React Data Structures - Architecture Level Review
Since you've built parser combinators and worked with Angular's digest cycle, you'll appreciate React's fundamentally different approach. Where Angular uses dirty checking and two-way binding, React treats UI as a pure function of state with unidirectional data flow.
Props Object
The props object is deceptively simple but has critical constraints. React calls Object.freeze() on the props object itself - but only at the top level. This means:
typescript
props.foo = 'bar';           // Runtime error - frozen
props.nested.foo = 'bar';    // Works! Only shallow frozen
props.array.push(item);      // Works! Array methods still function
Props are effectively a readonly contract at the TypeScript level, but at runtime they're shallow-frozen POJOs. The type you're generating with your mapped type Properties<T> is correct - extracting $-prefixed properties and adding children.
Critical detail: Props are recreated on every render, not mutated. When parent state changes, React creates an entirely new props object. This is why your attempt to add _chemicalId to props won't persist - next render gets a fresh object.
Children Prop
props.children is type ReactNode which is a discriminated union:
typescript
type ReactNode = 
    | ReactElement  // JSX element
    | string 
    | number 
    | ReactFragment // arrays
    | ReactPortal 
    | boolean 
    | null 
    | undefined
Children is exactly what's syntactically nested in JSX - no expansion, no resolution. If you write:
jsx
<Parent>
    <Child />
    {condition && <Other />}
</Parent>
Then props.children is literally that array/fragment. React doesn't process it until render. This is why your child binding approach needs to walk the children - they're just descriptors, not instances.
React Elements (what view() returns)
React elements are plain objects with this shape:
typescript
{
    type: string | ComponentType,  // 'div' or Counter
    props: object,
    key: string | null,
    ref: object | null,
    $$typeof: Symbol.for('react.element')  // Security marker
}
These are immutable descriptors, not DOM nodes or component instances. When you return JSX from your view(), you're returning these plain objects. React's reconciler later turns these into fibers and eventual DOM operations.
You can mutate the tree before returning it (as you're considering for child binding), but you must useReact.cloneElement() to create new element objects - the elements themselves are frozen.
Key Architectural Difference
Unlike Angular's components which are class instances with lifecycle hooks you can intercept, React components are just functions that React calls. The "instance" is React's internal Fiber node, not your component. This is why you need hooks - they're your only way to attach state to React's internal instance representation.
Your Chemistry framework is essentially creating a parallel instance system (via chemicalRegistry) that shadows React's internal one. The challenge is keeping them synchronized, which is why the subscription/update dance is so delicate.
Want to dive deeper into any of these structures, or shall we move to the next topic?

props.children is an array of 3 React elements: [Middle, Middle, Middle]
These are unopened descriptors - just {type: Middle, props: {...}, ...}
The first Middle has its own props.children containing the two Bottom elements
But Top doesn't see Bottom at all - they're nested inside Middle's props
In Middle's component function:
First Middle: props.children is array of 2 Bottom elements
Second & Third Middle: props.children is undefined
The key insight: children is only the immediate syntactic children. React doesn't expand or traverse anything. If you wrote:
jsx
<Top>
    <Middle />
</Top>
Then Top's props.children is the single element descriptor for Middle. Whatever Middle renders internally (even if it renders 100 Bottoms) is invisible to Top until Middle's component function actually executes.
What You Can Access in Component Function
Besides props, you can access:
Hooks state - Any state/refs/context you've set up via hooks
Closure variables - Anything in scope from parent closures
Global/module scope - Your registries, caches, etc.
Function parameters - Though React only passes props (and legacy context)
That's it. React deliberately keeps the component function interface minimal. No this, no instance methods, no lifecycle parameters. Everything else comes through hooks which tap into React's internal Fiber state.
The props are indeed read-only and you're correct - they're just input for rendering your view. The returned view is what React actually uses. The props object is discarded after the render (though React may hold references for diffing).
This is why your Chemistry framework's approach of maintaining a parallel instance system makes sense - React gives you almost nothing to work with directly.

Yes, exactly! You can transform the children tree using React's cloning utilities to create a new tree. This is a common and valid pattern.
Transforming Children
You can absolutely do this:
typescript
const transformedChildren = React.Children.map(props.children, (child) => {
    if (React.isValidElement(child)) {
        // Create new element with modified props
        return React.cloneElement(child, {
            ...child.props,
            extraProp: 'added',
            // Can even replace children
            children: transformChildren(child.props.children)
        });
    }
    return child;
});

return <div>{transformedChildren}</div>;
The key points:
React.cloneElement() creates a new element descriptor with merged props
The original elements are untouched (immutable)
You're building a new tree of descriptors
These modified elements become the children for your component's render
What This Means for Chemistry
For your child binding system, you could:
Walk incoming children in your Component function
Clone matching children with added props (like parent references)
Build your binding registry based on what you find
Return the transformed tree from view()
This is actually how many React libraries work - they intercept children, clone with modifications, and pass down context. For example:
typescript
// In your Component function
const boundChildren = React.Children.map(props.children, child => {
    if (React.isValidElement(child) && child.type.isChemical) {
        // Clone with parent binding
        return React.cloneElement(child, {
            __parentChemical: chemical,
            __bindingSlot: determineSlot(child)
        });
    }
    return child;
});
The cloned elements flow down as props to the child components, where they can read these added props and establish bindings.
This is perfectly valid React - you're not mutating, you're transforming immutable structures into new immutable structures. The reconciler handles the rest.

Component Function Parameters
No, React component functions receive exactly one parameter: props. That's it. You cannot add additional parameters that React will populate.
typescript
// This is ALL you get:
const Component: React.FC<Props> = (props) => { ... }

// You CANNOT do:
const Component = (props, state, context, refs) => { ... }  // ❌ React won't pass these
This is a fundamental constraint of React's design. Everything else comes through:
Hooks - Access React's internal state (useState, useContext, etc.)
Closure - Variables from parent scope
Module scope - Your registries, caches, singletons
Additional Data Structures Worth Knowing
Since you're building a framework, you should know about these internal structures (though you can't directly access them):
Fiber Nodes
React's internal representation of components. Each component instance has a Fiber with:
memoizedState - Linked list of hook states
memoizedProps - Props from last render
updateQueue - Pending state updates
alternate - Previous/WIP fiber for diffing
You can't access these directly, but understanding they exist explains React's behavior.
SyntheticEvent
React's cross-browser wrapper for native events:
typescript
onClick={(e: React.MouseEvent) => {
    e.nativeEvent  // Raw DOM event
    e.currentTarget  // Element with handler
    e.target  // Element that triggered
}}
Refs
When you need to escape React's model:
typescript
const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
// ref.current holds the actual DOM node or class instance
Context Value
The only way to pass data without props:
typescript
const value = useContext(MyContext);  // Whatever provider set
But again, these all come through hooks or props, not as parameters. React keeps the component interface deliberately minimal - it's just a pure function from props to elements.

ReactNode - The Universal Render Type
ReactNode is the union type for anything React can render. You encounter it everywhere:
typescript
// These all involve ReactNode:

useState<ReactNode>()  // Can store any renderable
view()  // Returns ReactNode
Where You Get ReactNode
From props.children - Whatever parent passed down
From JSX expressions - Any JSX evaluates to ReactNode
From React.Children utilities - When you map/iterate children
From your view() returns - What you return becomes ReactNode
Here's the key distinction:
typescript
// ReactElement - single JSX element descriptor
const element: ReactElement = <div>Hello</div>;

// ReactNode - can be element, string, array, null, etc.
const node1: ReactNode = <div>Hello</div>;
const node2: ReactNode = "plain string";
const node3: ReactNode = [<div/>, <span/>, "text"];
const node4: ReactNode = null;
const node5: ReactNode = 42;
Why This Matters for Chemistry
When you're processing children or building views:
typescript
// props.children is ReactNode - could be anything
if (React.isValidElement(props.children)) {
    // Now TypeScript knows it's ReactElement
    const elementChildren = props.children;
}

// React.Children handles ReactNode properly
React.Children.forEach(props.children, (child: ReactNode) => {
    // child could be element, string, number, null...
    if (React.isValidElement(child)) {
        // Now it's safe to check child.type, child.props
    }
});
The practical impact: your view() can return any of these types, and React will handle it. This is why you can return null to render nothing, or return an array of elements without wrapping in a fragment.
ReactNode is essentially "anything renderable" - it's React's most permissive type for render output.

ReactElement Interface
ReactElement is a plain object with this shape:
typescript
interface ReactElement {
    type: string | React.ComponentType;  // 'div' or MyComponent
    props: { [key: string]: any };       // Including children
    key: string | null;
    ref: any;
    
    // Internal fields (you don't touch these)
    $$typeof: symbol;  // Symbol.for('react.element')
    _owner: any;       // Fiber reference
}
When you write <div className="test">Hello</div>, you get:
javascript
{
    type: 'div',
    props: { className: 'test', children: 'Hello' },
    key: null,
    ref: null,
    $$typeof: Symbol.for('react.element')
}
ReactNode Type
ReactNode isn't an interface - it's a union type:
typescript
type ReactNode = 
    | ReactElement 
    | string 
    | number 
    | boolean 
    | null 
    | undefined
    | ReactNode[]  // Arrays of any of these
Cloning and Reassembly
Only ReactElements are cloneable via React.cloneElement():
typescript
// ✅ Can clone elements
const original = <div>Hello</div>;
const cloned = React.cloneElement(original, { className: 'new' });

// ❌ Cannot clone other ReactNodes
const text = "Hello";
React.cloneElement(text);  // ERROR - not an element
For non-element ReactNodes, you just use them directly or create new ones:
typescript
function transformChildren(children: ReactNode): ReactNode {
    if (React.isValidElement(children)) {
        // It's an element - can clone
        return React.cloneElement(children, { extra: 'prop' });
    }
    if (Array.isArray(children)) {
        // It's an array - map over it
        return children.map(transformChildren);
    }
    // String, number, null, etc. - just return as-is
    return children;
}
Where Elements Fit
Function components take props (which contain ReactNodes as children) and return ReactNode:
typescript
const Component: FC = (props) => {
    // props.children is ReactNode (could be elements, text, etc.)
    // Return value is ReactNode
    return <div>{props.children}</div>;  // This JSX creates a ReactElement
}
The JSX syntax creates ReactElements, which are a subset of ReactNode. So you're always working with ReactNode at the type level, but when you need to manipulate structure (clone, check type, access props), you narrow it down to ReactElement first.

What You Can Do With cloneElement
React.cloneElement() lets you:
typescript
React.cloneElement(
    element,
    props?,     // Merge new props (shallow merge)
    ...children // Replace children entirely
)
Specifically:
Merge props (shallow - doesn't deep merge)
Replace children completely
Change key
Change ref
You cannot change the type - if it's a div, it stays a div. To change type, create a new element.
Creating Elements From Scratch
Yes! You have three ways:
typescript
// 1. JSX (most common)
const elem = <div className="test">Hello</div>;

// 2. React.createElement
const elem = React.createElement('div', { className: 'test' }, 'Hello');

// 3. Just build the object (NOT recommended but works)
const elem = {
    $$typeof: Symbol.for('react.element'),
    type: 'div',
    props: { className: 'test', children: 'Hello' },
    key: null,
    ref: null
};
The third way is fragile (React could change internals) but shows it's just a plain object.
Practical Cloning Patterns
typescript
// Change props but keep children
const modified = React.cloneElement(element, { newProp: 'value' });

// Replace children entirely
const modified = React.cloneElement(element, null, 'new child');

// Deep clone with modified nested children
const deepClone = React.cloneElement(element, {
    ...element.props,
    children: React.Children.map(element.props.children, child => 
        React.isValidElement(child) ? React.cloneElement(child, { modified: true }) : child
    )
});

// Create entirely new element with same children
const wrapped = React.createElement('div', { className: 'wrapper' }, element);
The key limitation: cloneElement is shallow. If you need deep transformations, you manually walk and rebuild the tree.

Component Lifecycle - The Execution Model
In functional components, "lifecycle" is really about when code runs and what's safe to do when.
The Three Phases
1. Render Phase (Function Body)
What happens: React calls your component function When: Props change, state changes, parent re-renders, or initial mount
CAN DO ✅
Read props and state
Calculate derived values
Transform children
Return JSX
CANNOT DO ❌
Set state directly (infinite loop)
Subscribe to events
Modify DOM
Call side effects
Common Error:
typescript
const Component = (props) => {
    // ❌ ERROR: Cannot update during existing state transition
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    setCount(1);  // Dies here
}
Uncommon Pitfall:
typescript
const Component = (props) => {
    // Looks safe but isn't - this runs EVERY render
    const subscription = eventBus.subscribe(() => {});  
    // You're creating new subscriptions every render!
}
2. Commit Phase (After Render)
What happens: React updates the DOM and runs useLayoutEffect When: After render phase completes, before browser paint
This is synchronous - blocks painting. Use sparingly.
3. After Paint (useEffect)
What happens: useEffect callbacks run When: After browser has painted
CAN DO ✅
Set state (triggers new render)
Subscribe to events
Fetch data
Manipulate DOM
MUST DO ⚠️
Return cleanup function for subscriptions
Common Pitfall - Missing Dependencies:
typescript
useEffect(() => {
    doSomething(props.value);  // Uses props.value
}, []);  // ❌ Empty deps - won't re-run when props.value changes
Uncommon Pitfall - Cleanup Timing:
typescript
useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;
    
    async function load() {
        const data = await fetchData();
        // ❌ Component might have unmounted!
        if (!cancelled) setState(data);  // ✅ Check flag
    }
    
    return () => { cancelled = true; };
}, []);
The State Update Batching Trap
React 18 batches all state updates, but the timing can bite you:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const [a, setA] = useState(0);
    const [b, setB] = useState(0);
    
    const handleClick = () => {
        setA(1);
        console.log(a);  // Still 0! State updates are async
        setB(2);
        console.log(b);  // Still 0!
        // Both updates batch into ONE re-render
    };
}
The Closure Trap
The worst pitfall - stale closures:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    
    useEffect(() => {
        const timer = setInterval(() => {
            setCount(count + 1);  // ❌ count is always 0 here!
        }, 1000);
        
        return () => clearInterval(timer);
    }, []);  // Empty deps means count=0 is captured forever
}
Fix with functional update:
typescript
setCount(c => c + 1);  // ✅ Always gets current value
For Chemistry Framework
Your error "Cannot update during render" happens because you're subscribing during render phase. The fix is ensuring subscriptions happen in useEffect. Your current solution of storing the update function during render but subscribing in effect is close, but the subscription itself must be in the effect to avoid React's error detection.

Component Lifecycle - Correct Patterns
Let me clarify the actual lifecycle with proper terminology:
Phase 1: Render (Component Function Executes)
This happens before anything is in the DOM. React is just calling your function to get the ReactNode tree.
typescript
const Component = (props) => {
    // This code runs every render - before DOM exists
    // First render = "mount", subsequent = "updates"
    
    // ✅ CORRECT: Pure calculations
    const derived = props.value * 2;
    const transformed = React.Children.map(props.children, child => 
        React.isValidElement(child) ? React.cloneElement(child, {extra: true}) : child
    );
    
    return <div>{derived}</div>;
}
Phase 2: Commit (React Updates DOM)
After your function returns, React commits changes to the real DOM. You hook into this with useLayoutEffect:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
    
    useLayoutEffect(() => {
        // ✅ CORRECT: DOM exists but browser hasn't painted
        // Synchronous - blocks paint
        if (ref.current) {
            const width = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect().width;
            if (width > 500) {
                ref.current.style.fontSize = '20px';  // Change before user sees
            }
        }
    });  // No deps = runs after every commit
    
    return <div ref={ref}>Content</div>;
}
Phase 3: After Paint (useEffect)
Browser has painted. Safe for async operations:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const [data, setData] = useState(null);
    
    // ✅ CORRECT: Runs after FIRST paint only (mount)
    useEffect(() => {
        let cancelled = false;
        
        async function load() {
            const result = await fetchData();
            if (!cancelled) setData(result);
        }
        load();
        
        return () => { cancelled = true; };  // Cleanup on unmount
    }, []);  // Empty = mount only
    
    // ✅ CORRECT: Runs after EVERY paint
    useEffect(() => {
        console.log('Component painted with', props.value);
        // No cleanup needed for logging
    });  // No deps array = every paint
    
    // ✅ CORRECT: Subscribe with cleanup
    useEffect(() => {
        const handler = (e) => console.log(e);
        window.addEventListener('resize', handler);
        return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', handler);
    }, []);  // Mount only
}
Accessing Real DOM
Yes, you can access and manipulate the DOM, but do it through refs:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const divRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
    
    useEffect(() => {
        // ✅ CORRECT: Direct DOM manipulation when needed
        if (divRef.current) {
            // React doesn't know about these changes
            divRef.current.scrollTop = 0;
            
            // For libraries that need real DOM
            const chart = new ChartLibrary(divRef.current);
            return () => chart.destroy();
        }
    }, []);
    
    return <div ref={divRef} />;
}
Fixing the Previous Pitfalls
Stale Closure Fix:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    
    useEffect(() => {
        const timer = setInterval(() => {
            // ✅ CORRECT: Functional update
            setCount(c => c + 1);
        }, 1000);
        
        return () => clearInterval(timer);
    }, []);  // Empty deps OK because we use functional update
}
Subscription Fix:
typescript
const Component = (props) => {
    const [, forceUpdate] = useState({});
    
    useEffect(() => {
        // ✅ CORRECT: Subscribe in effect
        const subscription = eventBus.subscribe(() => {
            forceUpdate({});  // Trigger re-render
        });
        
        return () => subscription.unsubscribe();
    }, []);  // Resubscribe if these change
}
After Every Paint:
typescript
useEffect(() => {
    // This runs after EVERY paint
    console.log('Just painted');
});  // No dependency array = always runs
Mount means first render. There's no separate "mount" event - it's just the first time through these phases. DOM manipulation through refs is not hacky - it's the escape hatch for when you need it.

Detecting Mount
useEffect with empty deps is the mount detector:
typescript
useEffect(() => {
    console.log('MOUNTED!');
    return () => console.log('UNMOUNTING!');
}, []);  // Empty array = mount/unmount only
That's it. No need for flags - empty deps means "run once on mount".
Hooks - The Complete Picture
The Essential Four (90% of your needs)
useState - Local component state
typescript
const [value, setValue] = useState(initial);
const [value, setValue] = useState(() => expensiveInit());  // Lazy initial
useEffect - Side effects after render
typescript
useEffect(() => {
    // Runs after paint
    return () => {};  // Cleanup
}, [deps]);  // Rerun when deps change
useRef - Mutable reference that persists
typescript
const ref = useRef(initialValue);  // ref.current is mutable
const domRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);  // For DOM elements
useCallback/useMemo - Performance optimization
typescript
const memoizedFn = useCallback((arg) => {}, [deps]);  // Stable function reference
const memoizedValue = useMemo(() => expensive(), [deps]);  // Cached computation
The Contextual Ones
useContext - Consume context without Consumer component
typescript
const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
useReducer - Complex state with reducer pattern
typescript
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);
dispatch({type: 'INCREMENT'});
The Rarely Used
useLayoutEffect - Like useEffect but synchronous (blocks paint) useImperativeHandle - Expose methods to parent (with forwardRef) useDebugValue - Label custom hooks in React DevTools
Critical Hook Patterns
Pattern 1: Previous Value
typescript
function usePrevious<T>(value: T): T | undefined {
    const ref = useRef<T>();
    useEffect(() => {
        ref.current = value;
    });
    return ref.current;
}
Pattern 2: Force Update (for your Chemistry)
typescript
function useForceUpdate() {
    const [, forceUpdate] = useReducer(x => x + 1, 0);
    return forceUpdate;
}
Pattern 3: Event Handler with Stable Reference
typescript
function useEvent<T extends (...args: any[]) => any>(handler: T): T {
    const handlerRef = useRef(handler);
    handlerRef.current = handler;  // Always fresh
    
    return useCallback((...args) => {
        return handlerRef.current(...args);  // Call latest
    }, []) as T;  // But stable reference
}
Pattern 4: Subscription Management
typescript
function useSubscription<T>(
    subscribe: (callback: (value: T) => void) => () => void,
    deps: any[]
) {
    const [value, setValue] = useState<T>();
    
    useEffect(() => {
        return subscribe((newValue) => setValue(newValue));
    }, deps);
    
    return value;
}
The Rules (Never Break These)
Only call at top level - Never in conditions/loops
Only call in React functions - Components or custom hooks
Same order every render - React tracks by call order
Custom Hooks - Your Power Tool
typescript
// Encapsulate your Chemical binding logic
function useChemical<T extends $Chemical>(ChemicalClass: typeof $Chemical) {
    const [chemical] = useState(() => new ChemicalClass());
    const [, forceUpdate] = useState({});
    
    useEffect(() => {
        const unsubscribe = chemical.onUpdate.subscribe(() => forceUpdate({}));
        return unsubscribe;
    }, [chemical]);
    
    return chemical;
}
The key insight: Hooks let you compose behavior. Your Chemistry framework is essentially creating a custom state management hook that bridges your instance system with React's.

You're right to push back - I was being way too hand-wavy. Let me explain these properly.
useEffect Dependencies
typescript
useEffect(() => {
    console.log(props.value, localState);
}, [props.value, localState]);  // Dependencies array
Dependencies are the values your effect uses. React compares them between renders using Object.is(). If any changed, the effect reruns. If you lie about deps, you get stale closures:
typescript
// BAD - missing dep
useEffect(() => {
    console.log(count);  // Always logs 0 if count was 0 on mount
}, []);  // Should be [count]
useRef Explained
useRef must be called at component top level (hook rules). It returns an object with a current property:
typescript
const ref = useRef(0);
// ref is: { current: 0 }
// ref itself is stable, ref.current is mutable
You CAN mutate ref.current - that's the whole point:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const countRef = useRef(0);
    
    const increment = () => {
        countRef.current++;  // Mutate it! Won't trigger re-render
        console.log(countRef.current);  // Works fine
    };
    
    // Pass to functions
    doSomething(countRef);  // Pass the whole ref object
}
DOM Refs - The Real Explanation
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const divRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
    
    return <div ref={divRef}>Hello</div>;
}
Here's what happens:
useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null) creates { current: null } with TypeScript knowing current will eventually be an HTMLDivElement
When you pass ref={divRef} to a DOM element, React sets divRef.current to the actual DOM node after mounting
HTMLDivElement is the browser's DOM type (not React's) - it's the real div element with .style, .offsetWidth, etc.
useCallback Dependencies
typescript
const handleClick = useCallback((event) => {
    console.log(count);  // Captures count from closure
}, [count]);  // Recreate function when count changes
If count changes, useCallback returns a NEW function. Without it in deps, the function keeps using old count. Dependencies can be any value - React uses Object.is() comparison.
Context - The Actual Mechanism
Context is a way to pass data through the component tree without props:
typescript
// Create context
const ThemeContext = React.createContext({ dark: false });

// Provide value
<ThemeContext.Provider value={{ dark: true }}>
    <Child />
</ThemeContext.Provider>

// Consume in Child
const Component = () => {
    const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);  // { dark: true }
    
    // You get the object, but shouldn't mutate it
    theme.dark = false;  // BAD - mutating shared object
    
    // Instead, provider should offer a setter
}
useReducer - Properly Explained
typescript
// Reducer function YOU write
function reducer(state, action) {
    switch(action.type) {
        case 'INCREMENT':
            return { count: state.count + 1 };
        case 'DECREMENT':
            return { count: state.count - 1 };
        default:
            return state;
    }
}

const Component = () => {
    const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { count: 0 });
    
    // state is { count: 0 } - NOT like ref, it's immutable
    // dispatch calls YOUR reducer
    dispatch({ type: 'INCREMENT' });  // Calls reducer(state, {type: 'INCREMENT'})
}
useLayoutEffect vs useEffect
typescript
useLayoutEffect(() => {
    // Runs SYNCHRONOUSLY after DOM update, BEFORE paint
    element.scrollTop = 0;  // User never sees unscrolled position
});

useEffect(() => {
    // Runs AFTER paint
    element.scrollTop = 0;  // User might see flicker
});
Use useLayoutEffect when you need to measure/modify DOM before user sees it.
useImperativeHandle - Real Example
typescript
// Parent wants to call methods on child
const ChildInput = forwardRef((props, ref) => {
    const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
    
    useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
        focus: () => inputRef.current?.focus(),
        clear: () => { if(inputRef.current) inputRef.current.value = ''; }
    }));
    
    return <input ref={inputRef} />;
});

// Parent usage
const Parent = () => {
    const childRef = useRef();
    
    return (
        <>
            <ChildInput ref={childRef} />
            <button onClick={() => childRef.current.focus()}>Focus</button>
        </>
    );
}
Why forceUpdate Works
typescript
const [, forceUpdate] = useReducer(x => x + 1, 0);
useReducer returns [state, dispatch]
We ignore state (the ,)
Calling forceUpdate() runs the reducer x => x + 1
State changes from 0 to 1, then 1 to 2, etc.
Any state change triggers re-render
Custom Hooks - Where They Work
Custom hooks are just functions that call other hooks. They follow the same rules - only call at top level of components or other custom hooks:
typescript
// CAN'T do this
if (condition) {
    useSubscription(...);  // ERROR - conditional hook
}

// CAN do this
const result = useSubscription(...);  // Top level
if (condition) {
    use(result);  // Use the result conditionally
}

You're right - I'm not being precise enough. Let me answer your specific questions properly.
React's Dependency Comparison
React uses ␀0␀ comparison (like === but handles NaN and -0/+0 correctly). It's shallow - only one level:
typescript
// React's actual comparison logic (simplified)
deps.forEach((dep, i) => {
    if (!Object.is(dep, prevDeps[i])) {
        // Re-run effect
    }
});
So:
typescript
const obj = { count: 1 };
useEffect(() => {}, [obj]);  // Re-runs EVERY render because obj is new object each time

const [state] = useState({ count: 1 });
useEffect(() => {}, [state]);  // Never re-runs - state reference stable
useEffect(() => {}, [state.count]);  // Re-runs when count changes
DOM Ref Mutations
typescript
const divRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

// After mount, divRef.current is the actual DOM element
// You CAN mutate it directly:
divRef.current.style.color = 'red';  // Changes actual DOM
divRef.current.className = 'new';     // Changes actual DOM
divRef.current.scrollTop = 100;       // Scrolls element

// React doesn't track these changes - you're bypassing React
Context Setters Pattern
typescript
const ThemeContext = React.createContext({
    theme: { dark: false },
    setTheme: (theme: any) => {}  // Placeholder
});

// Provider component
const ThemeProvider = ({ children }) => {
    const [theme, setTheme] = useState({ dark: false });
    
    return (
        <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>
            {children}
        </ThemeContext.Provider>
    );
};

// Consumer
const Component = () => {
    const { theme, setTheme } = useContext(ThemeContext);
    setTheme({ dark: true });  // Call the setter
};
Refs ARE Mutable
typescript
const ref = useRef(0);
ref.current = 5;  // YES, you can mutate this!
console.log(ref.current);  // 5

// useReducer state is NOT mutable
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { count: 0 });
state.count = 5;  // This changes the object but doesn't trigger re-render
// Must use dispatch to trigger re-render
dispatch queues a state update. React calls your reducer either immediately or batched, then re-renders if state changed.
Effect Order
typescript
const Component = () => {
    console.log('1. Render');
    
    useLayoutEffect(() => {
        console.log('2. Layout effect - DOM updated, before paint');
    });
    
    useEffect(() => {
        console.log('3. Effect - after paint');
    });
    
    return <div>Hi</div>;
};
// Output: 1, 2, 3
The element in my example was sloppy - should be:
typescript
useLayoutEffect(() => {
    const element = document.getElementById('myDiv');
    element.scrollTop = 0;
});
useImperativeHandle Explained
forwardRef lets a component receive a ref prop:
typescript
// Without forwardRef, ref doesn't work on components
const MyInput = (props) => <input />;
<MyInput ref={ref} />  // ERROR - ref not accepted

// With forwardRef
const MyInput = forwardRef((props, ref) => {
    // ref is whatever parent passed
    return <input ref={ref} />;  // Attach to DOM
});
<MyInput ref={ref} />  // Works!

// useImperativeHandle customizes what ref.current becomes
const MyInput = forwardRef((props, ref) => {
    useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
        // ref.current will be this object
        focus: () => console.log('focusing'),
        value: 'custom'
    }));
    return <input />;
});
Hook Rules Are Strict
typescript
// React tracks hooks by ORDER
// First render: [useState, useEffect, useRef]
// Second render: [useState, useEffect, useRef]  // Must match!

if (condition) {
    useState();  // BREAKS - order changes based on condition
}
There's no use function in React - that was my typo. Should have been:
typescript
const result = useSubscription(...);
if (condition) {
    doSomething(result);  // Use the result

16:19 UTC, 4 September 2025
Props have a ref property available, but React treats it specially - it doesn't pass it down as a normal prop:
typescript
// Parent tries to pass ref
const Parent = () => {
    const myRef = useRef();
    return <MyComponent ref={myRef} />;
}

// Without forwardRef - ref is NOT in props
const MyComponent = (props) => {
    console.log(props.ref);  // undefined! React strips it out
    return <div />;
}

// With forwardRef - ref comes as second argument
const MyComponent = forwardRef((props, ref) => {
    console.log(props.ref);  // Still undefined
    console.log(ref);        // The ref from parent!
    return <div ref={ref} />;
});
React treats ref (and key) as special "reserved" props that it handles internally rather than passing through props. This is why you need forwardRef to access the ref in a function component - it's React's way of giving you access to this special prop.
For class components, ref automatically points to the component instance. But function components don't have instances, soforwardRef lets you decide what ref.current should be (via useImperativeHandle) or pass it to a DOM element.

Ref Types
No, refs don't have to be DOM refs. They can hold anything:
typescript
const dataRef = useRef({ count: 0 });
const timerRef = useRef<NodeJS.Timeout>();
const componentRef = useRef<MyComponentType>();
Why Not Check Function Signature?
JavaScript function serialization doesn't preserve parameter names reliably:
typescript
// After minification:
const Component = (a, b) => {...}  // Was (props, ref)

// Arrow vs regular functions serialize differently
const Arrow = (props, ref) => <div />;
Arrow.toString();  // "(props, ref) => <div />"

function Regular(props, ref) { return <div />; }
Regular.toString();  // "function Regular(props, ref) { return <div />; }"

// But minified:
const Arrow = (a,b)=>React.createElement("div");
React can't reliably detect if you want a ref parameter. Plus, checking function strings at runtime would be slow and break with minification.
React's approach is explicit - you opt into ref forwarding with forwardRef. This also makes it clear in the code that this component handles refs specially, rather than it being implicit based on parameter names.
Also, React needs to know at component definition time (not render time) whether to pass ref as a prop or second argument. forwardRef returns a different component type that React recognizes and handles specially.

Function Arity and Refs
React could theoretically check function .length for parameter count, but:
typescript
// These all have length 2
const A = (props, ref) => {};
const B = (props, context) => {};  // Old context API
const C = (a, b) => {};  // Minified

// Default parameters break .length
const D = (props, ref = null) => {};  // length is 1!

// Rest parameters
const E = (...args) => {};  // length is 0
Plus, React made this decision back when class components were primary - they needed a consistent API that worked for both.
Only One Ref
You can only pass one ref through the ref prop:
typescript
<MyComponent ref={singleRef} />  // Only one

// Want multiple refs? Use regular props:
<MyComponent ref={ref1} secondRef={ref2} thirdRef={ref3} />

// Or use callback refs to combine:
<MyComponent 
    ref={(el) => {
        ref1.current = el;
        ref2.current = el;
    }}
/>
The ref prop is singular - it's meant to represent "the" reference to this component, like how a variable has one memory address. If you need multiple refs, you pass them as normal props with different names.
forwardRef only forwards the single ref prop as the second parameter. Everything else stays in props.

State & Rendering - The Core Loop
Time to understand how React actually decides when and what to re-render, and how state is bound to component instances.
State Binding - Instance Isolation
Each component instance has its own state:
typescript
const Counter = () => {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    return <div>{count}</div>;
}

// In parent:
<>
    <Counter />  {/* Has count = 0 */}
    <Counter />  {/* Different instance, also count = 0 */}
</>
State lives in React's Fiber node for that component instance. When React unmounts and remounts a component (different position in tree), state is lost:
typescript
const Parent = () => {
    const [show, setShow] = useState(true);
    return (
        <>
            {show ? <Counter key="a" /> : null}
            {!show ? <Counter key="b" /> : null}  {/* New instance, fresh state */}
        </>
    );
}
Re-render Triggers (The Complete List)
State change - setState(newValue) where Object.is(old, newValue) is false
Parent re-renders - Always re-renders children (unless memoized)
Context value changes - All consumers re-render
Force update - Via forceUpdate() or reducer trick
Important: Props changing does NOT directly trigger re-render. Parent re-renders with new props, which causes child to re-render.
Render vs Commit
typescript
const Component = () => {
    console.log('Render phase - calculating');
    
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    const expensive = useMemo(() => {
        console.log('Computing expensive value');
        return count * 1000;
    }, [count]);
    
    useLayoutEffect(() => {
        console.log('Commit phase - DOM updated');
    });
    
    return <div>{expensive}</div>;
}
Render phase: React calls your component function. This might happen multiple times without committing (React can abort/restart renders).
Commit phase: React actually updates the DOM. Only happens if render phase produced different output.
Batching - The Hidden Optimizer
React 18 automatically batches ALL state updates:
typescript
// All three setState calls = ONE re-render
const handleClick = () => {
    setA(1);  // Doesn't render yet
    setB(2);  // Doesn't render yet  
    setC(3);  // Doesn't render yet
    // React renders ONCE here with all changes
}

// Even async!
const handleAsync = async () => {
    const data = await fetch('/api');
    setA(data.a);  // Still batched!
    setB(data.b);  // One render for both
}

// Force synchronous with flushSync
import { flushSync } from 'react-dom';
flushSync(() => {
    setA(1);  // Renders immediately
});
setB(2);  // Separate render
The Reconciliation Process
When you return new JSX, React compares ("reconciles") with previous:
typescript
// First render returns:
<div className="red">
    <span>Hello</span>
</div>

// Second render returns:
<div className="blue">
    <span>Hello</span>
    <p>World</p>
</div>

// React's reconciliation:
// 1. div same type, different props -> update className
// 2. span same type, same props -> no change
// 3. p is new -> insert DOM node
Key rule: Same component type at same position = same instance (preserves state).
The Bailout Optimization
React can skip rendering if nothing changed:
typescript
const Child = memo(({ value }) => {
    console.log('Child rendering');
    return <div>{value}</div>;
});

const Parent = () => {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    const [other, setOther] = useState(0);
    
    return (
        <>
            <Child value={count} />  {/* Only re-renders if count changes */}
            <button onClick={() => setOther(o => o + 1)}>Update other</button>
        </>
    );
}
Without memo, Child re-renders every time Parent does, even if props are identical.

Dependency Arrays - The Full Truth
Yes, React compares each element with Object.is():
typescript
// React's check (simplified)
const depsChanged = deps.some((dep, i) => !Object.is(dep, prevDeps[i]));
Different array lengths = always re-run:
typescript
// First render
useEffect(() => {}, [a, b]);     // 2 deps

// Second render  
useEffect(() => {}, [a, b, c]);  // 3 deps - ERROR!
This breaks the rules of hooks - you can't change the number or order of hooks between renders. The deps array itself must have consistent length.
Cleanup Functions - Where They're Used
Only useEffect and useLayoutEffect support cleanup:
typescript
useEffect(() => {
    // Setup
    return () => {
        // Cleanup - runs on unmount OR before next effect
    };
}, [dep]);
Cleanup runs in two situations:
Component unmounts
Dependencies change - cleanup runs BEFORE the new effect
typescript
useEffect(() => {
    console.log(`Subscribing to ${id}`);
    const sub = subscribe(id);
    
    return () => {
        console.log(`Unsubscribing from ${id}`);
        sub.unsubscribe();
    };
}, [id]);

// When id changes from 1 to 2:
// 1. "Unsubscribing from 1"  (cleanup)
// 2. "Subscribing to 2"      (new effect)
No other hooks support cleanup functions.
Custom Hooks - Yes, Just Functions
Custom hooks are exactly that - functions that use hooks:
typescript
// Custom hook - just a function starting with "use"
function useCounter(initial = 0) {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(initial);
    
    const increment = useCallback(() => {
        setCount(c => c + 1);
    }, []);
    
    return { count, increment };
}

// Usage
const Component = () => {
    const { count, increment } = useCounter(5);
    return <button onClick={increment}>{count}</button>;
}
The "use" prefix is a convention that:
Tells React's linter this follows hook rules
Makes it clear to other developers this contains hooks
Enables React DevTools to show custom hook state
That's it - they're just functions for sharing stateful logic. Your Chemistry framework could expose hooks like:
typescript
export function useChemical<T extends $Chemical>(ChemicalClass: new () => T): T {
    const [chemical] = useState(() => new ChemicalClass());
    const [, forceUpdate] = useState({});
    
    useEffect(() => {
        return chemical.onUpdate.subscribe(() => forceUpdate({}));
    }, [chemical]);
    
    return chemical;
}

Advanced React Patterns
Higher Order Components (HOCs)
An HOC is a function that takes a component and returns a new component with added behavior:
typescript
// HOC that adds logging
function withLogging<P extends object>(Component: React.ComponentType<P>) {
    return (props: P) => {
        useEffect(() => {
            console.log(`${Component.name} mounted`);
            return () => console.log(`${Component.name} unmounted`);
        }, []);
        
        return <Component {...props} />;
    };
}

// Usage
const Button = ({ onClick, children }) => <button onClick={onClick}>{children}</button>;
const LoggedButton = withLogging(Button);

// Now LoggedButton has logging behavior
<LoggedButton onClick={() => {}}>Click me</LoggedButton>
HOCs with Injected Props
More powerful - HOCs that provide props:
typescript
// HOC that provides auth state
function withAuth<P extends { user?: User }>(
    Component: React.ComponentType<P>
) {
    return (props: Omit<P, 'user'>) => {
        const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);
        
        useEffect(() => {
            fetchUser().then(setUser);
        }, []);
        
        // Inject user prop
        return <Component {...props as P} user={user} />;
    };
}

// Component expects user prop
const Profile = ({ user }: { user?: User }) => <div>{user?.name}</div>;

// Enhanced version doesn't need user passed
const AuthProfile = withAuth(Profile);
<AuthProfile />  // user injected by HOC
Render Props Pattern
Instead of HOCs, pass a function as children or prop:
typescript
// Mouse tracker using render prop
const MouseTracker = ({ render }: { render: (pos: {x: number, y: number}) => ReactNode }) => {
    const [pos, setPos] = useState({ x: 0, y: 0 });
    
    useEffect(() => {
        const handle = (e: MouseEvent) => setPos({ x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY });
        window.addEventListener('mousemove', handle);
        return () => window.removeEventListener('mousemove', handle);
    }, []);
    
    return <>{render(pos)}</>;
};

// Usage
<MouseTracker render={({ x, y }) => (
    <div>Mouse at {x}, {y}</div>
)} />

// Or using children as function
const MouseTracker2 = ({ children }: { children: (pos: {x: number, y: number}) => ReactNode }) => {
    // ... same logic
    return <>{children(pos)}</>;
};

<MouseTracker2>
    {({ x, y }) => <div>Mouse at {x}, {y}</div>}
</MouseTracker2>
Compound Components
Components that work together sharing implicit state:
typescript
const TabContext = React.createContext<{
    activeTab: string;
    setActiveTab: (tab: string) => void;
} | null>(null);

// Parent component
const Tabs = ({ children, defaultTab }: { children: ReactNode; defaultTab: string }) => {
    const [activeTab, setActiveTab] = useState(defaultTab);
    
    return (
        <TabContext.Provider value={{ activeTab, setActiveTab }}>
            <div className="tabs">{children}</div>
        </TabContext.Provider>
    );
};

// Child components that ONLY work inside Tabs
Tabs.List = ({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) => {
    return <div className="tab-list">{children}</div>;
};

Tabs.Tab = ({ id, children }: { id: string; children: ReactNode }) => {
    const context = useContext(TabContext);
    if (!context) throw new Error('Tab must be inside Tabs');
    
    return (
        <button 
            className={context.activeTab === id ? 'active' : ''}
            onClick={() => context.setActiveTab(id)}
        >
            {children}
        </button>
    );
};

Tabs.Panel = ({ id, children }: { id: string; children: ReactNode }) => {
    const context = useContext(TabContext);
    if (!context) throw new Error('Panel must be inside Tabs');
    
    return context.activeTab === id ? <>{children}</> : null;
};

// Usage - components work together
<Tabs defaultTab="tab1">
    <Tabs.List>
        <Tabs.Tab id="tab1">First</Tabs.Tab>
        <Tabs.Tab id="tab2">Second</Tabs.Tab>
    </Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Panel id="tab1">First content</Tabs.Panel>
    <Tabs.Panel id="tab2">Second content</Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>
Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
typescript
// Uncontrolled - component manages its own state
const UncontrolledInput = ({ defaultValue }: { defaultValue?: string }) => {
    const [value, setValue] = useState(defaultValue || '');
    return <input value={value} onChange={e => setValue(e.target.value)} />;
};

// Controlled - parent manages state
const ControlledInput = ({ value, onChange }: { value: string; onChange: (v: string) => void }) => {
    return <input value={value} onChange={e => onChange(e.target.value)} />;
};

// Hybrid - works both ways
const HybridInput = ({ value, defaultValue, onChange }: {
    value?: string;
    defaultValue?: string;
    onChange?: (v: string) => void;
}) => {
    const [internal, setInternal] = useState(defaultValue || '');
    const isControlled = value !== undefined;
    const current = isControlled ? value : internal;
    
    const handleChange = (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => {
        if (!isControlled) setInternal(e.target.value);
        onChange?.(e.target.value);
    };
    
    return <input value={current} onChange={handleChange} />;
};
Provider Pattern with Reducer
Complex state management pattern:
typescript
type State = { count: number; user: User | null };
type Action = 
    | { type: 'INCREMENT' }
    | { type: 'SET_USER'; user: User };

const StateContext = React.createContext<State | null>(null);
const DispatchContext = React.createContext<React.Dispatch<Action> | null>(null);

export const AppProvider = ({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) => {
    const [state, dispatch] = useReducer((state: State, action: Action) => {
        switch (action.type) {
            case 'INCREMENT': return { ...state, count: state.count + 1 };
            case 'SET_USER': return { ...state, user: action.user };
            default: return state;
        }
    }, { count: 0, user: null });
    
    return (
        <StateContext.Provider value={state}>
            <DispatchContext.Provider value={dispatch}>
                {children}
            </DispatchContext.Provider>
        </StateContext.Provider>
    );
};

// Custom hooks for using context
export const useAppState = () => {
    const state = useContext(StateContext);
    if (!state) throw new Error('Must be inside AppProvider');
    return state;
};

export const useAppDispatch = () => {
    const dispatch = useContext(DispatchContext);
    if (!dispatch) throw new Error('Must be inside AppProvider');
    return dispatch;
};
These patterns compose and combine - HOCs can use render props, compound components can be enhanced with HOCs, etc. The key is understanding when each pattern is appropriate for your abstraction needs.

Yes, children can be ANY ReactNode type, including functions!
typescript

<Container>
    <div>Normal child</div>
</Container>

<Container>

Understanding the Arrow Function Syntax
Let me break down this syntax:
typescript
{({ x, y }) => <div>Mouse at {x}, {y}</div>}
Step by step:
{...} - JSX expression wrapper
({ x, y }) - Function parameter with destructuring
=> - Arrow function
<div>...</div> - Return value
It's equivalent to:
typescript
{
    function(props) {
        const x = props.x;
        const y = props.y;
        return <div>Mouse at {x}, {y}</div>;
    }
}
TypeScript Props Destructuring
This syntax:
typescript

Is TypeScript destructuring with type annotation. Breaking it down:
typescript
// Version 1: Destructuring with inline type
const Component = ({ defaultValue }: { defaultValue?: string }) => {}

// Version 2: Same thing, with explicit type
type Props = { defaultValue?: string };
const Component = ({ defaultValue }: Props) => {}

// Version 3: Without destructuring
const Component = (props: { defaultValue?: string }) => {
    const defaultValue = props.defaultValue;
}
So when you see:
typescript

    {({ x, y }) => <div>Mouse at {x}, {y}</div>}
</MouseTracker>
MouseTracker receives children as a function. It calls that function with { x: 100, y: 200 }, and the function returns JSX.
The full flow:
typescript
const MouseTracker = ({ children }) => {
    const pos = { x: 100, y: 200 };
    
    // children is the function we passed
    // Call it with pos
    return children(pos);  // Returns <div>Mouse at 100, 200</div>
}

type Props = {

    // TypeScript enforces your schema

typescript
// Component that REQUIRES function children
interface RenderProps {
    isLoading: boolean;
    data: string[];
}

interface DataFetcherProps {
    url: string;
    children: (props: RenderProps) => ReactElement;  // MUST be function
}

const DataFetcher = ({ url, children }: DataFetcherProps) => {
    const [isLoading, setLoading] = useState(true);
    const [data, setData] = useState<string[]>([]);
    
    useEffect(() => {
        fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(d => {
            setData(d);
            setLoading(false);
        });
    }, [url]);
    
    // Call the function with our data
    return children({ isLoading, data });
}

// Usage - TypeScript enforces function

    {({ isLoading, data }) => 
        isLoading ? <Spinner /> : <List items={data} />

    <div>Not a function!</div>  // ERROR: Type 'Element' is not assignable to type '(props: RenderProps) => ReactElement'

17:01 UTC, 4 September 2025
Component Function Identity
The component function itself (the definition) never changes - it's the same function in memory:
typescript
const Counter = () => {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    return <div>{count}</div>;
}

// Counter === Counter always true
// It's the same function object
But React calls this function on every render, creating a new execution context each time:
typescript
// First render
Counter() // Called, creates scope with count=0

// State changes
Counter() // Called AGAIN, new scope with count=1

// Parent re-renders (even if Counter's props/state unchanged)
Counter() // Called AGAIN
Component Instance vs Function Calls
The "instance" (React's Fiber node) persists, but the function executes fresh each time:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    // This runs EVERY render
    console.log('Function called');
    
    // But state is preserved between calls by React
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    
    // This object is created new every render
    const obj = { value: count };
    
    // This ref persists across renders
    const ref = useRef();
    
    return <div>{count}</div>;
}
So:
Component function: Same function object always
Function execution: New call every render
Component instance (Fiber): Same as long as component stays in same tree position
State/refs: Preserved by React between function calls
Local variables: Created fresh each function call
This is why closures can be tricky - each render captures its own scope:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
    
    const handleClick = () => {
        setTimeout(() => {
            console.log(count); // Captures THIS render's count
        }, 3000);
    };
    
    // Click when count=0, then increment quickly
    // After 3 seconds, logs 0, not current count!
}
The function/instance relationship is: one function definition, multiple calls, one React Fiber instance (until unmounted).

React tracks component instances by position in tree and key:
typescript
<div>

    <Counter />  // Position 1 - different instance

    <Counter key="b" />  // Different instance

// Use a factory function

    const [id] = useState(() => nextId++);  // Lazy init, only runs once

    const id = useComponentId();
    console.log(`This instance is #${id}`);
    return <div>Instance {id}</div>;

typescript
import { useId } from 'react';

const Component = () => {
    const id = useId();  // Generates stable, unique ID like ":r1:"

typescript

    const [chemicalId] = useState(() => $Chemical.getNextChemicalId());

    let chemical = chemicalRegistry.get(chemicalId) as this;
    if (!chemical) {
        chemical = this.construct();
        chemical._id = chemicalId;
        chemicalRegistry.set(chemicalId, chemical);
    }

This gives each component instance a stable ID that persists across re-renders but is unique per mount.

State is destroyed on unmount, fresh on remount:

// Remount → count=0 again (fresh)

typescript
import { useId } from 'react';

typescript

React 18 batches ALL updates automatically:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const [a, setA] = useState(0);
    const [b, setB] = useState(0);

You can have as many as you want:
typescript

    // 20 different states? Sure
    const [s1, set1] = useState(0);
    const [s2, set2] = useState(0);
    // ... 18 more
    
    const updateAll = () => {
        set1(1);
        set2(2);
        // ... 18 more setters
        // Still just ONE re-render
    };
}
Even in Loops
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
    const [counts, setCounts] = useState({});
    
    const handleData = (data: Item[]) => {
        data.forEach(item => {
            setItems(prev => [...prev, item]);  // Called 100 times
            setCounts(prev => ({ ...prev, [item.id]: 0 }));  // Called 100 times
        });
        // Still batched into ONE re-render
    };
}
The only limit is memory - each setState call queues an update. But React processes them all together, so performance is fine.
For Chemistry, this means your multiple property updates all batch nicely into one re-render, which is why your framework works efficiently even when multiple properties change.

18:22 UTC, 4 September 2025
The problem is your subscription setup happens on every render, causing issues. Here's what's wrong:
typescript
// This runs EVERY render - bad!
if (chemical._updateToken)
    chemical.onUpdate.unsubscribe(chemical._updateToken);
const [, update] = useState({});
chemical._updateToken = chemical.onUpdate.subscribe(() => update({}));
You're unsubscribing and resubscribing on every render, which can cause the React state update warning.
Here's the corrected version:
typescript
private assignComponent(): void {
    const formula = this.getType().formula as this;
    const isFormula = this === formula;
    if (!isFormula && this._component) return

    const Component = (props: Properties) => {
        // Use lazy init to create chemical once
        const [chemical] = useState(() => {
            const c = this.construct();
            c._component = Component;
            return c;
        });
        
        // Set up update subscription
        const [, update] = useState({});
        
        useEffect(() => {
            // Subscribe AFTER mount, in effect
            const token = chemical.onUpdate.subscribe(() => update({}));
            chemical._updateToken = token;
            
            // Reactivate here, not during render
            chemical.reactivate();
            
            return () => {
                chemical.onUpdate.unsubscribe(token);
                chemical._onReceivingProps.clear();
                chemical._onRenderingView.clear();
                chemical._onRenderedView.clear();
                // Don't clear all onUpdate - just this subscription
            };
        }, [chemical]);  // Depend on chemical (stable reference)

        // Rest of component logic
        let newProps = chemical.onReceivingProps.fire(props);
        props = newProps || props;
        chemical.bindProps(props);
        
        let view = chemical.view();
        const result = chemical.onRenderingView.fire({ props, view });
        view = result?.view || view;
        chemical.onRenderedView.fire({ props, view });
        
        return view;
    }

    if (isFormula)
        formula._component = Component;
    if (!this._component)
        this._component = Component;
}
Key fixes:
Create chemical once with lazy state init
Subscribe in useEffect, not during render
Don't need ID tracking - the chemical instance is stable
reactivate() in effect, not during render

08:34 UTC, 5 September 2025
TypeScript Array Types - Full Flexibility
TypeScript arrays are incredibly flexible for typing:
typescript
// Fixed length tuples
type Pair = [string, number];
type Triple = [boolean, string, number];

// Variable length with specific positions
type AtLeastTwo = [string, string, ...string[]];
type FirstTwo = [ReactElement, ReactElement, ...ReactNode[]];

// Mixed types
type Mixed = (string | number)[];
type Components = (ReactElement<ButtonProps> | ReactElement<LinkProps>)[];

// Readonly arrays
type ReadonlyStrings = readonly string[];
type ReadonlyTuple = readonly [string, number];

// Named tuple elements (TS 4.0+)
type Range = [start: number, end: number];

// Conditional array types
type ArrayOrSingle<T> = T | T[];

// For children specifically
type ChildrenTypes = 
    | ReactElement<TabProps>  // Single specific element
    | [ReactElement<HeaderProps>, ReactElement<BodyProps>]  // Exact tuple
    | ReactElement[]  // Any number of elements
    | [ReactElement, ...ReactElement[]]  // At least one
Hooks That Must Run in Exact Order
ALL hooks must run in the same order every render. React tracks them by call order:
typescript
// First render hook order: [useState, useEffect, useRef]
const Component = ({ condition }) => {
    const [a] = useState();     // Hook #1
    
    if (condition) {
        const [b] = useState();  // ❌ BREAKS - sometimes hook #2, sometimes not there
    }
    
    useEffect(() => {});         // Sometimes #2, sometimes #3 - BROKEN
}
You CANNOT:
Add new hooks conditionally
Skip hooks conditionally
Change the order of hooks
Call hooks in loops with varying iterations
This is why the rule is "only call hooks at the top level."
The ref Prop Mechanism
The ref prop attaches a reference to either a DOM element or component instance:
typescript
const Component = () => {
    const divRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
    
    return <div ref={divRef}>Text</div>;
    // After mount, divRef.current is the actual DOM div element
}
How it works:
You pass a ref object (from useRef) to the ref prop
React sees the ref prop on a DOM element
After the DOM element is created, React sets ref.current to that element
On unmount, React sets ref.current back to null
For components, ref doesn't work unless they use forwardRef:
typescript
// Won't work - ref ignored
const MyComponent = (props) => <div />;
<MyComponent ref={ref} />  // ref not attached

// Works - forwardRef passes ref through
const MyComponent = forwardRef((props, ref) => <div ref={ref} />);
<MyComponent ref={ref} />  // ref attached to inner div
The ref prop is special - React intercepts it and doesn't pass it in props, similar to key.

11:22 UTC, 5 September 2025
That TypeScript won't compile. You can't have multiple rest elements in a tuple:
typescript
class X {
    // ❌ ERROR: A rest element cannot follow another rest element
    p: [string, ...string[], number, ...number[]] = ['a', 'b', 'c', 1];
}
TypeScript only allows ONE rest element, and it must be at the end:
typescript
// ✅ Valid patterns:
type A = [...string[]];                    // Any number of strings
type B = [string, ...number[]];            // String, then any numbers
type C = [string, number, ...boolean[]];   // String, number, then any booleans

// ❌ Invalid patterns:
type D = [...string[], number];            // Rest must be last
type E = [...string[], ...number[]];       // Only one rest allowed
If you need mixed types in the middle, use a union array:
typescript
class X {
    // All strings, then all numbers
    p: (string | number)[] = ['a', 'b', 'c', 1, 2, 3];
    
    // Or enforce structure with a function
    setP(strings: string[], numbers: number[]) {
        this.p = [...strings, ...numbers];

// Which gives: ReactNode[] (due to fallback)

Accept it as a limitation - children are runtime-validated in React, not compile-time validated by TypeScript.
