16:28 UTC, 5 September 2025
The fundamental issue you're encountering stems from how TypeScript's JSX type checking system operates at multiple layers, with special rules and transformations that differ from regular function call type checking. When you write JSX like <Component>{children}</Component>, TypeScript doesn't directly type-check this as a function call with props - it goes through a JSX transformation layer that has its own type resolution rules. The JSX namespace defines intrinsic elements and how component props are resolved, and crucially, the children prop gets special treatment where it's merged from multiple sources: the JSX.ElementChildrenAttribute interface, the component's props type, and React's default PropsWithChildren type application.
The reason function components with strictly typed children tuples work when called directly but not through JSX lies in TypeScript's JSX transformer implementation. When TypeScript sees JSX syntax, it doesn't just check if the props match the component's type signature - it first constructs a JSX.Element type, then checks if that element is assignable to the expected type. During this process, children undergo a specific transformation where they're collected into an array and typed as ReactNode[], regardless of what the component's actual props type specifies. This happens in the TypeScript compiler itself, not in the React type definitions, which means even perfectly typed components lose their children type specificity when used through JSX syntax.
React's type definitions compound this issue through their use of PropsWithChildren and defaultProps mechanisms. The React.FC type, which your Component type extends, automatically adds children?: ReactNode to props through PropsWithChildren, but even when you don't use FC and define props manually, the JSX transformer still treats children specially. The LibraryManagedAttributes type, which TypeScript uses to determine the final props type for JSX elements, performs transformations that can override or ignore custom children types. This is why your Properties type correctly preserves the $children type when accessed directly, but the JSX usage doesn't enforce it - the JSX transformer is operating at a different level with different rules.
The core architectural reason for this behavior relates to how JSX was designed to be a syntax sugar for React.createElement calls, which historically accepted children as variadic arguments after props. The type system has to accommodate both React.createElement(Component, props, child1, child2) and <Component>{child1}{child2}</Component> syntaxes, leading to a lowest-common-denominator approach where children are treated as ReactNode collections. TypeScript's JSX type checking predates many of the advanced type features like conditional types and template literal types, and the children handling hasn't been updated to leverage these newer capabilities for stricter typing.
Your Chemistry framework's approach of using a mapped Properties type is actually quite sophisticated and would work perfectly if TypeScript's JSX transformer respected it. The issue is that when TypeScript encounters <Test>, it looks up the JSX.IntrinsicElements for HTML elements or uses JSX.ElementClass for components, then applies LibraryManagedAttributes, which includes special handling for the children prop that bypasses your custom type. The transformation happens before your Properties type is even consulted for the children constraint, which is why the tuple type information is lost.
One critical detail is that TypeScript has different code paths for props type checking versus children type checking in JSX. Props go through the normal assignability checks where your types are respected, but children go through a separate collection and transformation process. The compiler collects all JSX children into an array, assigns them the type ReactNode[], and then checks if this array is assignable to the children prop type. However, this check is deliberately loose to accommodate the common pattern of conditional rendering and fragments, where the exact shape of children is dynamic.
The way TypeScript's compiler handles JSX children is hardcoded in the checker.ts file of the TypeScript compiler itself. When it encounters JSX children, it calls specific functions like getJsxElementChildrenPropertyName and elaborateJsxComponents that have special logic for the children prop. This logic predates much of TypeScript's modern type system and hasn't been updated to handle tuple types or complex union types for children. The compiler essentially treats children as a special case that bypasses normal type checking rules, which is why your tuple constraints aren't enforced.
Interestingly, there have been multiple proposals and discussions in the TypeScript GitHub repository about improving children type checking, but they've been complicated by backward compatibility concerns. Changing how children are type-checked would break a massive amount of existing React code that relies on the current loose behavior. The TypeScript team has been reluctant to make changes that would suddenly cause errors in previously working code, even if those errors would technically be correct according to the component's type definitions.
The React team has also contributed to this situation by historically encouraging loose children types. React's philosophy has been that components should be flexible about what children they accept, and strict children typing was seen as an anti-pattern. This cultural norm influenced how the TypeScript definitions for React were written, with children defaulting to ReactNode and most utilities assuming children can be any valid React content. Only recently has there been more acceptance of strictly typed children for specific use cases like compound components.
A potential workaround that some libraries use is to bypass JSX entirely for components that need strict children typing. Instead of using JSX syntax, they provide builder functions or factory methods that construct the element tree with full type safety. This approach works because it avoids the JSX transformer entirely, but it sacrifices the ergonomics and familiarity of JSX syntax. Your Chemistry framework could potentially offer both approaches - JSX for convenience and builder methods for strict typing.
Another approach some teams have taken is to use branded types or nominal typing for children, where the children type includes a unique symbol or brand that makes it incompatible with regular ReactNode. This forces TypeScript to pay attention to the type mismatch, but it requires wrapping all children in special wrapper components or using type assertions, which significantly complicates the API. The overhead of this approach often outweighs the benefits of compile-time children checking.
The most pragmatic solution many libraries adopt is to combine loose compile-time types with strict runtime validation. They accept that TypeScript won't enforce their children constraints through JSX and instead validate children in the component implementation. This approach provides good developer experience through clear runtime errors while avoiding fights with TypeScript's JSX transformer. Your Chemistry framework could enhance this with development-mode validation that's stripped in production builds.
Looking at how other frameworks handle this, Vue's JSX implementation actually does a better job of preserving slot types (their equivalent of children), and SolidJS has made different architectural choices that allow for stricter typing. These frameworks benefited from being designed after TypeScript became mainstream, allowing them to build their JSX transformations with typing in mind from the start. React's JSX transformation was designed before TypeScript existed, and the type definitions were retrofitted onto an existing runtime behavior.
The ultimate issue is that fixing this properly would require changes to TypeScript's compiler itself, not just type definitions. The JSX transformer would need to be updated to respect custom children types, preserve tuple types through the transformation, and properly thread type information from the component definition to the JSX usage site. This is technically feasible but would require coordination between the TypeScript team, the React team, and the broader ecosystem to manage the breaking changes.
For your Chemistry framework, the most practical path forward is likely to accept this limitation and design around it. You could provide excellent runtime validation with clear error messages, offer alternative strictly-typed builder APIs for cases where compile-time safety is critical, and document this as a known TypeScript limitation rather than a Chemistry bug. The framework's value isn't diminished by this TypeScript quirk, and users who understand the limitation can work effectively within it.

The error message reveals the problem! TypeScript thinks you're trying to use Component<$Empty> (which is a React component type) as a child element, but you're actually passing a ReactElement.
The issue is that Component<$Empty> is the type React.FC<Properties<$Empty>> - a function component type, not an element. When you write <Empty />, you get a ReactElement, not a Component.
Your explicit typing shows the confusion:

This says "I expect a div element and a Component function", but you're actually passing:

    T extends keyof JSX.IntrinsicElements ? ReactElement<JSX.IntrinsicElements[T]> :
    T extends $Chemical ? ReactElement<Properties<T>> :  // Add this

Not Component types, but ReactElement types - which is what JSX actually produces.

Accept this as a TypeScript limitation

                this._isValue = false;
                this._symbolizer = symbolize;
            }

    }

        if (!(value instanceof this._type))
            throw new Error(`${this._property} must be an instance of ${this._type.name}`);
    }

    private static nextBondId = 1;
    private static getNextBondId(): number { return $Bond.nextBondId++; }
}

    private static getNextBondId(): number { return $Bond.nextBondId++; }
}

Bond Property Configuration Logic
The Bond class manages how properties become reactive in the Chemistry framework. Here's how each property gets configured:
Configuration Flow
Constructor Phase: Bond is created with a property name and chemical instance
Configure Phase: Walks the prototype chain from most general (Object/Chemical prototype) to most specific (instance)
Examine Phase: At each level, the bond accumulates characteristics from:
Decorators (only on prototypes): @parent, @inert, @dynamic, @$
Property Descriptors: Detects getter/setter patterns
Value Analysis: Infers type from actual values
How Properties Get Their Values
From Decorators (Prototype Level):
@parent: Makes property return the chemical's parent, overrides everything else
@inert: Marks property as non-reactive
@dynamic: Sets custom symbolizer for deep equality checks
@$: Configures Chemical binding with type and requirement level ('!', '?', '[]')
From Descriptors:
Read-only properties (getter without setter): Marked as non-settable and mutable
Computed properties (getter+setter): Preserve original functions
From Value Analysis:
Primitives (string/number/boolean): Use reference equality
Objects/Arrays: Use deep equality via symbolizer
Chemical instances: Track as Chemical with reference equality
Key Methods:
configure(): Initial full prototype chain walk
refresh(): Re-examines only the instance level (for runtime changes)
reactivate(): Creates the reactive property descriptor with get/set interceptors
double(): Clones bond for a new chemical, preserving configuration but getting new ID
The bond encapsulates all the reactive behavior - tracking changes, triggering updates, and managing the property lifecycle.

I've simplified the Bond class significantly:
Removed descriptor storage - Not needed since we create it fresh
Stored getValue/setValue on the bond - This allows the property descriptor to use arrow functions that capture this (the bond), making it reusable when doubled
Used arrow functions in property descriptor - They capture the bond instance, so when we double(), the new bond's methods are used
Added freeze() method - Simply sets _isInert = true
Simplified examine() - Removed redundant checks and initialization logic
Reorganized - Private methods below public, static at bottom
The key insight for duplication is storing _getValue and _setValue on the bond instance. When we create the property descriptor with arrow functions, they capturethis (the bond), so the doubled bond can reuse the same pattern with its own backing field and methods.

I've made the key improvements for performance and doubling:
Added generic ␀0␀ for property type - Allows type-safe access to values
Added ␀0␀ getter/setter - Direct, fast access to the property value on the chemical without going through descriptors
Stored descriptor - The PropertyDescriptor is saved so it can be reused/cloned
Optimized ␀0␀ - Only checks the current value type, doesn't walk prototype chain
Improved ␀0␀:
Uses Object.create(this) for efficient prototype-based cloning
Copies the current value to the new chemical's backing field
Reactivates to create a new descriptor bound to the new chemical
Stored ␀0␀ and ␀1␀ - These are created once during reactivate and reused
The key for performance is that refresh() now only examines the current value, not the whole prototype chain. And double() efficiently clones using prototypal inheritance, only creating new backing fields and descriptors as needed.
The value getter/setter provides fast direct access without going through the reactive descriptor, which is useful for internal operations that don't need reactivity.

import React, { ReactNode, ReactElement, useState, useRef, useEffect } from 'react';
import stringify from 'fast-safe-stringify';

// Core framework types
type Constructor<T = {}> = new (...args: any[]) => T;
type Type<T = any> = Constructor<T>;
type Component<T = any> = React.FC<Properties<T>>;
type OptionalComponent<T = any> = React.FC<OptionalProperties<T>>;

type Properties<T = any> = {
    [K in keyof T as K extends `$${infer Rest}` ? Rest : never]: T[K]
} & {
    children?: ReactNode;
};

type OptionalProperties<T = any> = {
    [K in keyof T as K extends `$${infer Rest}` ? Rest : never]?: T[K]
} & {
    children?: ReactNode;
};

interface Setter<T extends $Chemical = $Chemical> {
    (value: T): void;
    instance?: $Chemical;
}

// Symbols on $Chemical
const decoratorsKey = Symbol('decoratorsField');

// Global registry for Chemical instances by key
const chemicalRegistry = new Map<Component, $Chemical>();

class DecoratorCache {
    $: Map<string, { type: Type, expecting: '?' | '!' | '[]' }> = new Map();
    parent: Map<string, Type> = new Map();
    inert: Map<string, boolean> = new Map();
    dynamic: Map<string, ((value: any) => any) | undefined> = new Map();
}

// A decorator for expressing configurable binding
export function $(type: Type, expecting: '?' | '!' | '[]' = '!') {
    type = resolveType(type);
    if (!(!type || type === $Chemical || type.prototype instanceof $Chemical))
        throw new Error(`$ decorator expects a $Chemical class instead of ${type?.name}`);
    return function (target: $Chemical, property: string) {
        const dynamicTarget: any = target;
        if (!dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey])
            dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey] = new DecoratorCache();
        const decorators: DecoratorCache = dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey];
        decorators.$.set(property, { type: type, expecting: expecting });
    };
}

// A decorator for reassigning the parent property
export function parent(type?: Type) {
    return function (target: $Chemical, property: string) {
        if (!type) type = $Chemical;
        const dynamicTarget: any = target;
        if (!dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey])
            dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey] = new DecoratorCache();
        const decorators: DecoratorCache = dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey];
        decorators.parent.set(property, type);
    };
}

// Decorator to mark a field as inert (non-reactive)
export function inert() {
    return function (target: any, property: string) {
        const dynamicTarget: any = target;
        if (!dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey])
            dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey] = new DecoratorCache();
        const decorators: DecoratorCache = dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey];
        decorators.inert.set(property, true);
    };
}

// Decorator for properties that should use deep equality comparison
export function dynamic(symbolizer?: (value: any) => any) {
    return function (target: any, property: string) {
        const dynamicTarget: any = target;
        if (!dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey])
            dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey] = new DecoratorCache();
        const decorators: DecoratorCache = dynamicTarget[decoratorsKey];
        decorators.dynamic.set(property, symbolizer || symbolize);
    };
}

📚 Core Hooks (Essential)
[ ] useState - Adds state to functional components; returns [value, setter] pair
[ ] useEffect - Runs side effects after render; handles lifecycle events like mount/unmount
[ ] useMemo - Memoizes expensive computations; recalculates only when dependencies change
[ ] useCallback - Memoizes functions to prevent recreation on every render
[ ] useRef - Creates mutable reference that persists across renders without triggering re-renders
[ ] useContext - Accesses React context values without prop drilling
📦 Data Structures
[ ] Props object - Immutable object passed from parent; frozen at top level only
[ ] Children prop - Special prop containing nested JSX; can be elements, strings, arrays, or undefined
[ ] React elements - Plain objects describing what to render; created by JSX or React.createElement
[ ] React nodes - Valid render values: elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null, undefined
🔄 Component Lifecycle
[ ] Mount phase - Component first appears; state initialized, first render, effects run
[ ] Update phase - Props/state change triggers re-render; cleanup then re-run effects
[ ] Unmount phase - Component removed; cleanup functions run, refs cleared
💾 State & Rendering
[ ] State binding - State is bound to component instance, not globally
[ ] Re-render triggers - State changes, prop changes, parent re-renders, context changes
[ ] Render phase vs commit phase - Calculate what changed vs actually update DOM
[ ] Batching - React groups multiple state updates into single re-render
🎯 Advanced Patterns
[ ] Rules of Hooks - Only call at top level, only in React functions
[ ] Dependency arrays - Control when effects/memos recalculate
[ ] Cleanup functions - Return from useEffect to clean up subscriptions/timers
[ ] Custom hooks - Extract component logic into reusable functions

Refactored $Bond Class v1
typescript
// Bond Configuration Logic Analysis:
//
// The Bond class encapsulates how a property becomes reactive. The logic flow:
// 
// 1. CONSTRUCTOR: Creates bond with property name and chemical instance
// 2. CONFIGURE: Walks prototype chain from most general to most specific:
//    - Starts at Object/Chemical prototype
//    - Works down to the actual instance
//    - Each level can add/override bond characteristics
// 3. EXAMINE: At each prototype level, checks:
//    - Decorator cache (only on prototypes) for @parent, @inert, @dynamic, @$ decorators
//    - Property descriptors for getter/setter patterns
//    - Actual values to infer type characteristics
// 4. REFRESH: Re-examines only the instance level for runtime changes
// 5. REACTIVATE: Creates the reactive property descriptor that intercepts get/set
// 6. DOUBLE: Clones bond for a new chemical instance, preserving configuration

class $Bond<T = any> {
    get id() { return this._id; }
    private _id: number;
    get chemical() { return this._chemical; }
    private _chemical: T;
    get descriptor() { return this._descriptor; }
    private _descriptor?: PropertyDescriptor;
    get type() { return this._type; }
    private _type?: Type;
    get property() { return this._property; }
    private _property: string;
    get isInitialized() { return this._isInitialized; }
    private _isInitialized: boolean;
    
    get isParent() { return this._isParent; }
    private _isParent = false;
    get isChemical() { return this._isChemical; }
    private _isChemical = false;
    get isMutable() { return this._isMutable; }
    private _isMutable = false;
    get isValue() { return this._isValue; }
    private _isValue = false;
    get isCollective() { return this._isCollective; }
    private _isCollective = false;
    get isSettable() { return this._isSettable; }
    private _isSettable = true;
    get isRequired() { return this._isRequired; }
    private _isRequired = false;
    get isInert() { return this._isInert; }
    private _isInert = false;
    get isProp() { return this._isProp; }
    private _isProp = false;
    get isDelayed() { return this._isDelayed; }
    private _isDelayed = false;
    get isImplicitlyBound() { return this._isImplicitlyBound; }
    private _isImplicitlyBound = false;
    get isExplicitlyBound() { return this._isExplicitlyBound; }
    private _isExplicitlyBound = false;
    get symbolizer() { return this._symbolizer; }
    private _symbolizer: (value: any) => any = (value) => value;
    
    private _isReactive = true;
    get isReactive() { return this._isInert ? false : this._isReactive; }
    set isReactive(value: boolean) { this._isReactive = value; }
    get isPolled() { return this._isMutable || !this._isSettable; }

    constructor(property: string, chemical: T) {
        this._id = $Bond.getNextBondId();
        this._chemical = chemical;
        this._property = property;
        this._isInitialized = false;
        this._isReactive = false;
        this.configure();
    }

    private configure() {
        // Build prototype chain from most general to most specific
        const prototypes: any[] = [];
        let proto = this._chemical;
        while (proto) {
            prototypes.unshift(proto);
            if (proto === $Chemical.prototype) break;
            proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(proto);
        }
        
        // Walk from general to specific, building up bond characteristics
        for (const prototype of prototypes) {
            this.examine(prototype, prototype === this._chemical ? 'instance' : 'prototype');
        }
    }

    private examine(target: any, mode: 'instance' | 'prototype') {
        // Check decorator cache on prototypes
        if (mode === 'prototype') {
            const decorators = target[decoratorsKey];
            if (!decorators) return;
            
            // @parent decorator
            const parentType = decorators.parent.get(this._property);
            if (parentType) {
                this._type = parentType || $Chemical;
                this._isParent = true;
                this._isChemical = true;
                this._isInert = true;
                this._isSettable = false;
                return; // Parent overrides everything else
            }
            
            // @inert decorator
            const inert = decorators.inert.get(this._property);
            if (inert) this._isInert = true;
            
            // @dynamic decorator
            const dynamic = decorators.dynamic.get(this._property);
            if (dynamic !== undefined) {
                this._symbolizer = dynamic || symbolize;
                this._isMutable = true;
            }
            
            // @$ decorator for Chemical bindings
            const $config = decorators.$.get(this._property);
            if ($config) {
                this._type = $config.type;
                this._isProp = this._property.startsWith('$');
                this._isChemical = true;
                
                // Handle expecting parameter
                if ($config.expecting === '[]') {
                    this._isCollective = true;
                    this._isRequired = true;
                    // Initialize empty array if needed
                    const chemical = this._chemical as any;
                    const value = chemical[this._property];
                    if (value && !Array.isArray(value)) 
                        throw new Error(`${this._property} marked array but isn't`);
                    if (!value) chemical[this._property] = [];
                } else {
                    this._isRequired = $config.expecting === '!';
                    if ($config.expecting === '?' && Array.isArray(target[this._property]))
                        throw new Error(`${this._property} optional but is array`);
                    
                    // Initialize required Chemical with placeholder
                    if (this._isRequired && this._isChemical && !target[this._property]) {
                        const formula = (this._type as any).example || (this._type as any).prototype;
                        const chemical = this._chemical as any;
                        chemical[this._property] = Object.create(formula);
                        chemical[this._property]._reactive = false;
                    }
                }
                
                // Check for explicit binding
                if (this._isProp) {
                    const chemical = this._chemical as any;
                    const baseName = this._property.substring(1);
                    if (chemical[baseName] === $Chemical.$set) {
                        this._isExplicitlyBound = true;
                    } else {
                        this._isImplicitlyBound = true;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        
        // Check property descriptor for getter/setter
        const descriptor = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(target, this._property);
        if (descriptor?.get && !descriptor.set) {
            this._isSettable = false;
            this._isMutable = true;
            if (!this._symbolizer || this._symbolizer === ((v: any) => v))
                this._symbolizer = symbolize;
        }
        
        // Examine value to infer type characteristics
        const value = descriptor?.get ? undefined : target[this._property];
        if (value === null || value === undefined) return;
        
        if (value instanceof $Chemical) {
            this._isChemical = true;
            this._isValue = true;
            this._isMutable = false;
            this._symbolizer = (v) => v;
            if (!this._type) this._type = value.constructor as Type;
            return;
        }
        
        const valueType = typeof value;
        if (valueType === 'string' || valueType === 'number' || valueType === 'boolean') {
            if (!this._isValue && !this._isMutable) {
                this._isValue = true;
                this._symbolizer = (v) => v;
            }
            return;
        }
        
        if (valueType === 'object') {
            if (this._isCollective && !Array.isArray(value))
                throw new Error(`${this._property} is collective but got non-array`);
            if (!this._isCollective && Array.isArray(value) && this._isRequired)
                throw new Error(`${this._property} got unexpected array`);
            
            if (!this._isMutable) {
                this._isMutable = true;
                this._isValue = false;
                this._symbolizer = symbolize;
            }
        }
    }

    refresh() {
        // Only re-examine the instance level, not prototypes
        this.examine(this._chemical, 'instance');
    }

    deactivate(chemical: $Chemical) {
        if (chemical === chemical.getType().example)
            throw new Error('Examples should not have activated properties');
        this._isReactive = false;
    }

    reactivate(chemical: $Chemical): any {
        if (chemical === chemical.getType().example)
            throw new Error('Examples should not have activated properties');

        if (this._isInitialized) {
            this._isReactive = true;
            return;
        }

        if (this._isParent) {
            console.log(`Creating ${chemical.getType().name}.${this._property} as parent`)
            this._descriptor = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(
                Object.defineProperty(chemical, this._property, {
                    get() { return chemical.parent; },
                    enumerable: true,
                    configurable: false,
                }),
                this._property
            );
            this._isInitialized = true;
            return;
        }

        const thisBond = this;
        const chemical$: any = chemical;
        const backingField = Symbol(`_${this._property}${this._id}`);
        const existingDescriptor = Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(chemical$, this._property);
        const getValue = existingDescriptor?.get ?

        }
        
        const value = descriptor?.get ? undefined : target[this._property];
        if (value == null) return;
        
        if (value instanceof $Chemical) {
            this._isChemical = true;
            this._isValue = true;
            this._isMutable = false;
            this._symbolizer = (v) => v;
            if (!this._type) this._type = value.constructor as Type;
            return;
        }
        
        const valueType = typeof value;
        if (valueType === 'string' || valueType === 'number' || valueType === 'boolean') {
            if (!this._isValue && !this._isMutable) {
                this._isValue = true;
                this._symbolizer = (v) => v;
            }
            return;
        }
        
        if (valueType === 'object') {
            if (!this._isMutable) {
                this._isMutable = true;
                this._isValue = false;
                this._symbolizer = symbolize;
            }
        }
    }

    private checkType(value: any): void {
        if (!this._type || !this._isChemical || value == null) return;
        if (!(value instanceof this._type))
            throw new Error(`${this._property} must be an instance of ${this._type.name}`);
    }

    private static nextBondId = 1;
    private static getNextBondId(): number { return $Bond.nextBondId++; }
}
